primary_meaning: Prideful human rebellion against God (exalting self/city to heaven without God), producing confusion, scattering, and judgment; more broadly the archetypal worldly empire/system (idolatrous, immoral, oppressive) that captivates and persecutes God's people and stands opposed to His kingdom, destined for divine overthrow.
primary_basis: Genesis 10:8-12; 11:1-9 (Nimrod, Tower of Babel, name 'Babel' = confusion)
2 Kings 24–25; Daniel 1–5 (Babylonian conquest, exile, royal pride)
Revelation 14:8; 16:19; 17–18 (Babylon the Great, the harlot city, fallen)

alternatives.meaning: Code name or symbol specifically for imperial Rome (and its culture/power)
basis: Revelation 17–18 details (seven hills, worldwide commerce, persecution of saints) matching first-century Rome

alternatives.meaning: False/apostate religion or ecclesiastical system (often historicist Protestant identification with papal Rome or institutional Christendom)
basis: Revelation 17 (harlot with cup of abominations, riding the beast, drunk with saints' blood)
Reformation-era and later historicist readings of the same passages

alternatives.meaning: Literal future/rebuilt Babylon (or end-times geopolitical/economic system centered on a revived Babylon) in dispensational or futurist readings
basis: Literalist interpretation of Isaiah 13, Jeremiah 50–51, and Revelation 18 as still-future

alternatives.meaning: General symbol of any oppressive human culture, empire, or 'city of man' (Augustine) versus the city of God, without fixed historical identification
basis: Broader 'two cities' tradition in Christian theology

alternatives.meaning: Origin of pagan mystery religions or source of all false religion (popularized by certain 19th-century polemics)

notes: Broad Christian consensus holds that Babel/Babylon functions as the paradigmatic symbol of human pride and the anti-God world system; historical and confessional traditions differ mainly on concrete identification (Rome, ecclesiastical structures, future entity) rather than the core symbolic valence. Babel and Babylon are routinely treated as continuous in name, origin, and meaning.
